title: Essential phrasal verbs
goal: Student knows and uses 30 essential phrasal verbs and understands separable vs inseparable.
module_chunks: get up / wake up / go out / come in / sit down / stand up
turn on / turn off / put on / take off
look for / look after / look at / look up
find out / give up / pick up / put down
run out of / get along with / come up with / put off
bring up / carry out / fall through

units.title: Daily phrasal verbs
units.grammar_focus: Daily routine phrasal verbs (get up, wake up, go out)
units.real_life_context: You describe your daily routine using phrasal verbs.

grammar.explanation: "Get up" = leave bed. "Get on" = enter (bus). "Get out" = leave.

grammar.sentence: Please _____ the light when you leave.
grammar.explanation: "Turn off" = switch off. "Turn on" = switch on.
"Take off" = remove. Opposite of "put on".

grammar.sentence: I _____ my coat before going out.
grammar.explanation: "Put on" = wear. Opposite of "take off".

grammar.sentence: Please _____ the TV — I want to watch the news.
grammar.explanation: "Turn on the TV" — common chunk.
"Go out" = leave home (often for social activity).
Sometimes simple verbs work too. "Left the meeting".

grammar.sentence: I get up early everyday at 6.
grammar.answer: I get up early every day at 6.
grammar.explanation: "Every day" (two words) is the time phrase. "Everyday" (one word) is an adjective meaning routine.

grammar.hint: pronoun goes BETWEEN turn and on (separable)
grammar.explanation: With pronouns, separable phrasal verbs split: "turn IT on", not "turn on it".

grammar.passage: I get up at 6, put on my workout clothes, and go out for a run. When I come back, I turn on the coffee maker.
grammar.question: What does the speaker put on?
grammar.explanation: The text says "put on my workout clothes".

listening_speaking.text: I get up at 6 every day.

units.title: Look for, look after
units.grammar_focus: Phrasal verbs with "look" (look for, look after, look at, look up)
units.real_life_context: You use "look" phrasal verbs to describe searching, caring, checking.

grammar.explanation: "Look for" = search for. "Look after" = take care of. "Look at" = observe.
"Look after" = take care of.
"Look at" = direct attention to.

grammar.sentence: I'll _____ that word in the dictionary.
grammar.explanation: "Look up" = search information (dictionary, internet).
"Looking for a job" — searching.

grammar.sentence: Can you _____ my dog while I'm away?
grammar.explanation: "Look after my dog" — take care.

grammar.sentence: I _____ the painting for a long time.
grammar.explanation: "Looked at" — past form, observed/admired.
"Look FOR" = search. Missing "for" is common error.
For caring, "look after", not "look for".

grammar.passage: I'm looking for my phone. My sister looks after my kids on weekends. I always look up words I don't know.
grammar.question: Who looks after the kids?
grammar.explanation: The text says "My sister looks after my kids".

listening_speaking.text: She looks after her sister's kids.

units.title: Find out, give up, pick up
units.grammar_focus: Phrasal verbs of discovery, ending, fetching
units.real_life_context: You describe discovering information, quitting, and fetching things.

grammar.explanation: "Find out" = discover. Past: "found out".
"Give up" = quit. Past: "gave up".

grammar.sentence: Can you _____ my brother at the airport?
grammar.explanation: "Pick up" = collect/fetch someone.

grammar.sentence: She _____ her phone on the table.
grammar.explanation: "Put down" = place down.
Past simple of "find out".
"Gave up coffee" = stopped drinking.
"Pick you up" (or "pick up you" — but "you" between).

grammar.sentence: I picked up him at the station.
grammar.answer: I picked him up at the station.
grammar.explanation: Pronoun goes BETWEEN: "picked him up", not "picked up him".

grammar.sentence: She found that I was late.
grammar.answer: She found out that I was late.
grammar.explanation: "Find out" = discover info. "Found" alone = located physically.

grammar.passage: I found out about the party yesterday. I'll pick you up at 8. Don't give up trying!
grammar.question: When will the speaker pick you up?
grammar.explanation: The text says "I'll pick you up at 8".

listening_speaking.text: Can you pick me up at 7?

units.title: Separable vs inseparable
units.real_life_context: You correctly position pronouns with separable phrasal verbs.

grammar.explanation: With pronoun, separable phrasal verb splits: "turned IT off".
"Look after" inseparable — pronoun goes after the phrasal: "look after her".
Pronoun between: "picked HIM up".
"Look after" inseparable. Pronoun goes AFTER the whole phrasal verb.
With noun, can separate: "turn the music off" OR "turn off the music". Both correct.
With pronoun "me", separated: "pick me up".

grammar.sentence: She looks _____ her dog every day.
grammar.explanation: "Look after" inseparable. "After her dog".
Separable phrasal verb with pronoun: split. "Picked ME up".
"Look after" is inseparable — never split, even with pronoun.

grammar.passage: I turned the TV off. Can you pick me up at 7? She looks after her dad every weekend.
grammar.question: When should they pick the speaker up?
grammar.explanation: The text says "pick me up at 7".

units.title: Phone English
units.grammar_focus: Phone English in Inter register — phrasals and expressions for business calls (Fase B extra unit)
units.real_life_context: You handle phone calls professionally — identifying yourself, transferring, taking messages, dealing with bad connections.

grammar.explanation: "Hello, this is [name]" — standard professional phone identification in English. Never "I am [name]" or "my name is [name]" when answering — those work in person but not on the phone. "This is" is the convention.
"Can I speak to [person]?" — standard professional request. Slightly more formal: "May I speak to [person]?". "Could I speak to [person]?" also works. All three are polite phone register.
"Yes, speaking" — concise phone-specific confirmation that you are the person being asked for. Fixed phone convention. "Yes, it's me" works casually but "speaking" is more professional.

"I'll put you through" — phrasal verb meaning "transfer". Fixed phone English. "Put you through to [department]" or just "put you through" (when context is clear). Common in receptionist/secretary speak.

grammar.sentence: She's on _____ line right now. Can I take a message?
grammar.hint: indefinite article + word for telephone connection
grammar.explanation: "She's on another line" / "She's on the other line" — phone English for "she's busy with another call". "Another line" suggests there are multiple; "the other line" implies a specific second line.
"We were cut off" — phrasal verb for losing phone connection. Passive voice — the connection cut us off, we didn't do it ourselves. Fixed phrase: "I think we were cut off" / "Sorry, we got cut off".

"I'll get back to you" — phrasal verb for "I'll respond later" or "I'll follow up". Standard professional phone close when you can't answer immediately. Different from "call you back" (which means literally make another call).

"My name is" is for face-to-face introductions; on the phone, the convention is "This is [name]". Cross-cultural error: in many languages, the personal pronoun is used; English phone English uses "this".

grammar.sentence: Wait a moment, please. I'll pass you.
grammar.hint: "Put you through" is the phone phrasal
grammar.answer: Wait a moment, please. I'll put you through.
grammar.explanation: "Pass you" doesn't mean transfer in English phone register. The fixed phrasal is "put you through". Other phone English phrasals: "hang up" (end call), "hang on" (wait), "call back" (return call).

grammar.passage: Hello, this is Maria speaking. Can I speak to Pedro, please? Oh, he's on another line. Can you take a message? Please tell him to call me back when he's free. My number is 555-1234. Thanks — sorry, I think we're being cut off. I'll get back to you later. Bye!
grammar.question: What two phone-specific phrasal verbs appear?
grammar.answer: "cut off" (connection lost) and "get back to" (respond later). Also: "call me back" (return call), "speak to" (talk with).
grammar.explanation: Phone English vocabulary: "this is...speaking" (identification), "speak to" (talk with), "on another line" (busy), "take a message" (record), "call back" (return call), "cut off" (lose connection), "get back to" (respond later). Each is a fixed phone convention.

listening_speaking.text: Can I speak to Pedro, please?
I'll get back to you tomorrow.
